comments.text:
Now its easier to speak with hindsight now, and things have changed of course. But I will still criticise, for educational purposes, the video:
1. This build is wholly 'High-End'. Everything apart from he gpu is. Thats like calling the RX 6700xt 'High-end'. Nah, its a solid but budget 1440p card.
2.  You didn't say how much each part costs and total build cost. This is huge as people need to truly see the Cpu-Gpu imbalance. If you di an I5-12600k with the A770, THAT WOULD MAKE so much more sense (sorry didn't mean caps).
3. You really aren't supposed to front mount an AIO. Yes it works, but more dust gets towards the fans. Moreover (idk the exact science) but the cables are less optimised that way too.
4.. When doing the final shots of the completed build (14:45) , the 2 top fans are the wrong way round.
5. You only tested 1 game my friend. Yes time constraints and all that. But you tested ONE game. Come on now everyone else tests a good several and at 2 different resolutions. Hell even if you didn't have time to test at 1080p testing say 5 games at 1440p would have been actually a good test of the PC.
But I hope since its been a while now you know do these things. As well as doing: XMP profiles for ram, using Cinebench to test CPU etc.

Now its easier to speak with hindsight now, and things have changed of course. But I will still criticise, for educational purposes, the video:
1. This build is wholly 'High-End'. Everything apart from he gpu is. Thats like calling the RX 6700xt 'High-end'. Nah, its a solid but budget 1440p card.
2.  You didn't say how much each part costs and total build cost. This is huge as people need to truly see the Cpu-Gpu imbalance. If you di an I5-12600k with the A770, THAT WOULD MAKE so much more sense (sorry didn't mean caps).
3. You really aren't supposed to front mount an AIO. Yes it works, but more dust gets towards the fans. Moreover (idk the exact science) but the cables are less optimised that way too.
4.. When doing the final shots of the completed build (14:45) , the 2 top fans are the wrong way round.
5. You only tested 1 game my friend. Yes time constraints and all that. But you tested ONE game. Come on now everyone else tests a good several and at 2 different resolutions. Hell even if you didn't have time to test at 1080p testing say 5 games at 1440p would have been actually a good test of the PC.
But I hope since its been a while now you know do these things. As well as doing: XMP profiles for ram, using Cinebench to test CPU etc.

comments.text:
Now its easier to speak with hindsight now, and things have changed of course. But I will still criticise, for educational purposes, the video:
1. This build is wholly 'High-End'. Everything apart from he gpu is. Thats like calling the RX 6700xt 'High-end'. Nah, its a solid but budget 1440p card.
2.  You didn't say how much each part costs and total build cost. This is huge as people need to truly see the Cpu-Gpu imbalance. If you di an I5-12600k with the A770, THAT WOULD MAKE so much more sense (sorry didn't mean caps).
3. You really aren't supposed to front mount an AIO. Yes it works, but more dust gets towards the fans. Moreover (idk the exact science) but the cables are less optimised that way too.
4.. When doing the final shots of the completed build (14:45) , the 2 top fans are the wrong way round.
5. You only tested 1 game my friend. Yes time constraints and all that. But you tested ONE game. Come on now everyone else tests a good several and at 2 different resolutions. Hell even if you didn't have time to test at 1080p testing say 5 games at 1440p would have been actually a good test of the PC.
But I hope since its been a while now you know do these things. As well as doing: XMP profiles for ram, using Cinebench to test CPU etc.

comments.text:
Now its easier to speak with hindsight now, and things have changed of course. But I will still criticise, for educational purposes, the video:
1. This build is wholly 'High-End'. Everything apart from he gpu is. Thats like calling the RX 6700xt 'High-end'. Nah, its a solid but budget 1440p card.
2.  You didn't say how much each part costs and total build cost. This is huge as people need to truly see the Cpu-Gpu imbalance. If you di an I5-12600k with the A770, THAT WOULD MAKE so much more sense (sorry didn't mean caps).
3. You really aren't supposed to front mount an AIO. Yes it works, but more dust gets towards the fans. Moreover (idk the exact science) but the cables are less optimised that way too.
4.. When doing the final shots of the completed build (14:45) , the 2 top fans are the wrong way round.
5. You only tested 1 game my friend. Yes time constraints and all that. But you tested ONE game. Come on now everyone else tests a good several and at 2 different resolutions. Hell even if you didn't have time to test at 1080p testing say 5 games at 1440p would have been actually a good test of the PC.
But I hope since its been a while now you know do these things. As well as doing: XMP profiles for ram, using Cinebench to test CPU etc.

comments.text:
Just to clarify: JayzTwoCentz has an in-depth video explaining why it's not a big deal to mount a radiator as shown in this video.

TL;DR: the concern that an orientation causes is an air bubble getting into the pump, but mounted like this, the tubing is above the pump, meaning the air physically cannot travel to the pump.

No it's not the ideal orientation, but it's not bad by any measure.

Simply flip the radiator around 180 degrees to the tubes go to the bottom of the case (not physically possible i know but bear with me) and that would allow air to travel to the pump, which will kill it. That's the way you're not supposed to mount AIO liquid cooling

comments.text:
@Jay-ik1pt  Correct, though I should add that there are three pump locations that should be noted when installing. The traditional Asetek pump, where the pump is in the CPU block, is where you don't want the radiator at the bottom of the case, or if front mounted, the radiator to be mounted towards the bottom (240mm rad on a case where 3 120mm fans are supported at the front, for example).

The second is where the pump is in the middle of the radiator, like some from NZXT, Fractal, or even those MSI ones that are going bad. Front and bottom mounting are fine, but top mounting will lead to trouble, since the rad, and therefore the pump, will end up at the top.

Finally, there's those Be Quiet! AIOs, where the pump is on the tubes. Front mounting, unless you can mount it tubes down comfortably, is where the trouble will be caused. And that depends on the size of the rad, the case, and how big your graphics card is. Bottom or top mounting will be perfectly fine, since either the pump head, or the radiator itself, will be the top of the loop, and not the pump. If you're using a 120mm version, and are rear mounting, make sure the tubes are mounted down, so the pump doesn't end up at the top of the loop.

tl;dr, just pay attention to where the pump is on your AIO, and make sure it's not at the top of the loop.
comments.author: @mclytesabr666

comments.text: @mclytesabr666  Yep absolutely. The simplest way to say it is just "do not allow the pump to be the highest part of the loop". ...and, I suppose, if you want it to be silent then ideally the rad end-tank on the opposite end from the tubes should be the highest point but that's harder to achieve in a lot of builds and far less important.

comments.author: @nothingyetimstillgoing

comments.text: @nothingyetimstillgoing  No, he's telling you that "low profile" is not a description for heatsink size or power consumption. A low profile PCI/PCIe card is a special type of card with a smaller PCB that is about half height and has a shorter PCI bracket, or can be converted to a shorter bracket. Low profile cards are sometimes used in small form factor builds or small desktop style cases where regular cards cannot fit. The Intel A770 is a regular full height card.

comments.text:
Most things can only be plugged in in one way, for most other things where you can plug it in in multiple ways, it doesn't really matter which way you do it. For the things that does matter, there's lots of guides that does cover it. The reason most videos skips that part, is that it can easily take as long or longer to get some nice cable managing, as it does to build the whole rest of the computer. Can't really do a 30+ minute computer building video where 25mins of the video is just cable management. It'd kill your stats for that video, which affects how your future videos are recommended to others.
Really, to see things like that, you kind of have to go to smaller channels. It's just the sad truth of how YouTube works.

comments.text: Sorry to be that guy. But I can't help but mention that it's probably better to put those tubes at the top than the bottom.  Look at it this way: there is or will be (once time acts to steal some fluid from the loop) an air bubble at the highest point in the loop. Your job is to keep that air bubble away from the pump (which will pretty quickly burn up and die if it is not water-cooled). By putting those tubes going up from the pump, you reduce the likelihood that the air bubble will land right at pump level as it can rise into those tubes. If the tubes are below the pump, then the volume of fluid above the pump goes down and you have less air-bubble-tolerance in your build.

comments.text:
It's easier to build a PC now than it was 10+ yrs ago. I'm not saying it was difficult before, but building a PC today feels like playing Legos. We have the convenience of NVME m.2 SSDs which are super fast. Before we had to RAID 0 multiple bulky 3.5" HDD to achieve high read and write speed. Cable management is easier now because of modular power supplies and minimal cable use, no need for molex, sata, ata, ide, etc.
We have power supply covers built-in in most cases. I had to DIY my covers by cutting and bending plexiglass and wrapping them in vinyl sheets to match the case. Also, RGB lights are pretty common now. Before, it wasn't a gaming PC if it didn't have Cold Cathode Lights. 🤣🤣

Considering the connections on the radiator are at the highest point of the system it will mean that they are at a point where the air is accumulating and a part of this air will get sucked down into the pump again. It's not the worst, the worst is if the pump is the highest point and the air accumulate in the pump. The best is if the side of the radiator without connections is the highest point. So okay install for sure.

Is the Intel Arc Intel’s first foray into dedicated graphics? 
Also, is that A770 their best card? What’s the comparable?
comments.author: @ChrisbeFoSerious

comments.text:
It's Intel's first serious line of graphics cards, I think there have been some light mobile cards in the past. I don't know if the A770 is broadly available yet, but it should roughly compare to an Nvidia RTX 3060 from what I've read. There are still driver issues with the Arc GPUs, they only perform competitively with newer (DirectX 12) games, which is probably why Forza was the showcase in this video.
For model naming, Intel are actually using a pretty sensible scheme - A is for the first generation, the next number is the product tier (currently 3, 5 or 7, just like their i3/i5/i7 CPUs, and they haven't announced a 9 tier this generation). So the A770 is the highest-tier one that's currently available, and they're not trying to compete directly with the high-end cards from AMD and Nvidia.
I think it's cool to see more competition in the GPU space, even though it's probably going to take a generation or two before Intel cards actually make sense to buy for normal gamers.

comments.text:
I believe the tubes from the AIO cooler are actually supposed to be at the top, never at the bottom.

That’s why you can mount it at the top of the case as well.
comments.author: @RealDr_Gottlieb

comments.text:
Wrong, tubes should be at the bottom with a front mount. Otherwise you get more noise due to air bubbles which always accumulate at the top thanks to buoyancy, so in a radiator you don't want that to be where the inlet/outlet ports are. Even worse if the pump is the highest point of your loop in such configuration, because it increases the chance of it running dry, and that's very, very bad. 

Marques acknowledges this, he had no choice due to what AIO he had to work with and how the case is constructed. It's nothing catastrophic to do it the way he's done it, but it's sub-optimal for noise and maybe temperatures a little bit.
comments.author: @neoqueto

Thanks for explaining!
